en: Śrī:
The Second Chapter of the Nyāyakusumāñjali.
Thus, when a non-worldly cause has been established in this general manner, there must necessarily be a means for its accomplishment.
And that [reality] cannot be seen by people such as ourselves;
nor can there be any practical discourse (*vyavahāra*) regarding what is unseen. Therefore, it is possible that there exists a supramundane being who experiences everything.
(71) Now, one might argue that the tradition of the Dharma must proceed either through the eternal and faultless Vedas, or through an omniscient being perfected by yoga and ritual action.

If it is asked, "What is the use of postulating a Supreme Lord?"—to this it is replied: Because valid cognition is dependent [on other factors], because creation and dissolution are possible, and because there is no confidence in anything other than that, no other alternative is possible. (1)
For it is thus: [the cognition of error] depends on a cause over and above the causes of valid cognition, because, while being an effect, it is a particularity thereof, just like invalid cognition.
And if it were dependent on those [causes of valid cognition] alone, then even invalid cognition would be valid cognition itself.
For there exists a cause for knowledge therein;
otherwise, even knowledge would not arise from it.

If it is argued that, despite being knowledge, it is non-valid because of the intrusion of an additional defect, then in that case, valid knowledge would also arise only by depending on the additional factor of the absence of defects.
Because it necessarily depends upon that.
If it is argued: "Let there be the additional absence of defects; however, their presence is not admitted"—this might indeed be so.

If it were necessarily the case that defects must consist exclusively of positive entities (*bhāvarūpa*), this would not be so; for even non-existence (*abhāva*), such as the non-perception of distinguishing features (*viśeṣādarśana*) and the like, functions as a defect.
Otherwise, how could doubt and error arise from it?
Therefore, since that non-existence is itself a positive state, why is it not accepted as such?
It might be argued: "In the case of verbal testimony (*śabda*), defects such as a desire to deceive are indeed positive states;

therefore, in their absence, verbal knowledge is valid by its own nature. This is not so, because in inference (*anumāna*) and other means of knowledge, there are [defects] such as the misapprehension of the logical mark (*liṅga*).
Even if defects (*doṣa*) were [the cause] of cognitions, valid cognition would not arise merely through their absence.
If it is argued: "Let it be as it may in other cases;

however, in the case of verbal testimony (*śabda*), there is no dependence on the speaker's excellences (*guṇa*) when there is an absence of intent to deceive and so forth," we say no—because the opposite argument is equally applicable: that in the absence of excellences, the invalidity of that [cognition] does not depend on the speaker's defects (*doṣa*).

If it is argued that defects possess positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with respect to invalidity, we say no; for positive and negative concomitance exist for excellences (*guṇa*) with respect to validity as well. [Kumārila 2.206] Let this rule apply to the case of human-authored texts. But in the case of non-human (Vedic) texts, validity arises solely from the cessation of defects—if this is argued, we say no; for invalidity is also possible through the cessation of excellences.
If it is argued that its capacity regarding invalidity has not been perceived—then where has the capacity for validity regarding the cessation of defects been perceived?
If you say "in the speech of worldly people," the case is the same:
when there is invalidity in that [speech], defects alone are the cause.
If it is argued that the cessation of defects is simply the unavoidable presence of [excellences], this applies equally to excellences with respect to validity.
If it is argued that the presence of excellences is necessitated by the removal of defects, let it be granted that the presence of defects is likewise necessitated by the removal of excellences.
If it is argued that in this way the Veda would be devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) because it is not of human origin, then you must blame yourself.

Therefore, although [the absence of] aversion and attachment is invariably concomitant with them, because the efforts of engagement and withdrawal necessarily conform to attachment and aversion, these efforts have attachment and aversion as their causes;
however, it is not the case that the effort of withdrawal has aversion alone as its cause.

However, even though the effort toward activity is accompanied by attachment, it is logical to distinguish it as being caused by the absence of aversion; for there is no difference [in this regard]. The same applies here as well.
Nevertheless, once the non-human origin of the Vedas is established, their authority will be proven precisely because they are free from the defects of a speaker.
Therefore, once validity (*prāmāṇya*) is established, since that [validity] exists even in the absence of excellences (*guṇa*), the absence of defects (*doṣa*) alone is the cause;
if it is argued that excellences are not the cause, we say no, because it would follow that there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) based on the absence of the speaker's excellences.
[Thus,] the determination of validity is indeed intrinsic (*svataḥ*).
However, by this [statement], mere doubt is removed;
for since that [doubt] is based on a defect, it ceases when that defect is absent.
Therefore, this is not like inference (*anumāna*).
If it is argued that it is proper to provide a counter-argument (*sat-pratisādhana*), we say no; for a doubt based on the cessation of excellences (*guṇa*) is easily accessible.

If it is argued that such a doubt does not arise because the mere absence of excellences is not a factor for invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*), then it is equally true that the mere absence of defects (*doṣa*) is not a factor for validity (*prāmāṇya*), and thus there can be no removal of doubt by that alone.
Thus, validity is known extrinsically (*parataḥ*) because, in the state of non-habituation, it is subject to doubt, just like invalidity.

If, however, validity were known intrinsically, there would never be any doubt regarding its validity, just as there is no doubt regarding its being a cognition; for once something is ascertained, such doubt has no occasion to arise.

For this [doubt] does not arise merely from the perception of common characteristics and so forth, while disregarding the absence of any means of valid cognition that either establishes or subverts [the object];
for if that were the case, it would follow that such doubt could never be eliminated.

[Ku. 2.209] Now, the intention is that doubt arises because, just as with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such a cognition is observed even in the case of an invalid one, and no distinction between them is perceived. Is it then the case that, even when a cognition produced by a means of valid cognition is apprehended, its validity is not apprehended, or rather that the cognition produced by a means of valid cognition itself is not apprehended? In the first case, how can there be a grasping of validity intrinsically (*svataḥ*)?
Because even when the condition (pratyaya) is perceived, that [object] is not perceived.
In the second case, how could there be any doubt regarding it?
For the very locus (dharmin) is not apprehended.
As for the claim that intrinsic validity (*svataḥ prāmāṇya*) is asserted because immediate and abundant purposeful activity would otherwise be inexplicable—
that too is not the case, since it is explicable in another way.
For immediate activity, being inexplicable without the prompt occurrence of its causes, [requires those causes].
One should reject that [objection]:
even though activity occurs abundantly, it depends on the abundance of its own causes;
and desire is the cause of activity.
The cause of that [desire] is also the cognition that [the object] is a means to a desired end.
That too arises from the experience of a mark (liṅga) consisting in its belonging to the same class [as other known means].
And that [experience] is born from sense-object contact and so forth.
However, the apprehension of validity has no utility whatsoever;
or, if it does have utility, why is it said to be "self-evident" (*svataḥ*)?
Therefore, even the abundance of successful activity results either from the abundance of validity or from the abundance of its apprehension; but where is the utility of its being self-evident?
For indeed, the fact that the activity of those who are thirsty toward water is both immediate, abundant, and effective does not constitute a perception of its power to alleviate thirst.
This might be argued: all of this is possible only when the apprehension of validity exists;
and if that were not intrinsic (svataḥ), [how could it be so]?

If it is argued that [the validity of knowledge] would simply not exist because the opponent's position is untenable due to infinite regress—[we reply]: no, for even in the absence of such apprehension, everything is possible through doubt regarding the object;
nor is there indeed an infinite regress, since we do not accept that validity must necessarily be known.

Otherwise, this same problem would apply even to the position that [knowledge] is self-evident (*svataḥ*). If it is argued that a logical mark (*liṅga*) must be ascertained in order to be a means of ascertainment, and that this necessitates a dependence on another logical mark for its own ascertainment, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*); then does not an object that is logically impossible (*anupapadyamāna*) imply its own justifier (*upapādaka*) even while it remains unascertained?

If it is argued that there is no infinite regress because the [existence of the cognition] is ascertained by perception, and because that [perception] is an ascertainment precisely through its own existence— then this is equal for me as well, since the logical mark (*liṅga*) is ascertained by perception, and that [ascertainment] is an ascertainment precisely through its own existence.
Thus, the two cases are the same.

If it is asked, "How can there be a determination of that [sign] (i.e., the sign-determination) if the validity of the cognition of the sign has not been ascertained?"—then it is the same for the cognition of an impossible object: how can there be its determination if the validity of that cognition has not been ascertained?
For perception does not determine its object either by means of a [subsequent] ascertainment or by means of an ascertainment of its own validity.
If it is argued that it was stated "[the probans exists] by its own existence," that is equal [to our position].

Furthermore, if even so that were a fallacious mark (*liṅgābhāsa*), what would happen? If even an impossible object were to be a fallacy, [then the distinction between valid and invalid cognition would collapse].

"In that case, what is the news?"—the point is the same. It is a general rule (*utsarga*) that even that [inference] implies validity; and if it is argued that this is set aside (*apodyate*) in some cases by a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), then the same applies to the inferential mark (*liṅga*) as well. Thus, the situation is equal.

If it is argued that, "In that case, even in the inference for validity (*prāmāṇyānumāna*), doubt remains in the same state, and thus the effort is fruitless," this too is exactly the same. There is some such object that is logically untenable which would not be a mere appearance even in a dream; therefore, one should not doubt. If this is said, the resolution is the same: the same applies to the logical mark (*liṅga*) as well.
[ku.2.215] But what is this object which would not even appear in a dream—
that non-perception of which allows for the possibility of error? (77)
And the establishment of its sublation depends upon such a perception;
for otherwise, even if it were of that nature, if there were deviation [from the truth], that [sublation] would not exist either.
If you say, "Let it not be so," we reply: no, for there must be a distinction between reality and unreality (the establishment of reality and unreality).
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction.
For how could there be a superimposition of the opposite even when all specific features that determine [the object] have been perceived?
Or, if such were the case, how could there be a sublation when no specific feature beyond those has been perceived?
"But in the absence of that [sublation], how can there be error for one who is unsublated?

[To this, it might be argued: "Even if validity were extrinsic (*parataḥ*), since the Vedas are eternal, they possess independence; and since they are accepted by great people (*mahājana*), they possess validity—what contradiction is there?"
No; for neither of the two [positions] is established.
For it is not the case that the phonemes themselves are eternal.
To explain: "The letter *ga* heard previously does not exist now. (It does exist.)
"The clamor has ceased"— thus the destruction of sound is perceived by direct perception itself.
For it is not the case that the sound itself has gone elsewhere,
since it is formless (amūrta).
Nor is he obstructed,
precisely because in that case a severance of the connection would be impossible;
nor is the listener inattentive.
Because it is not perceived even when there is attention;
nor is the sense faculty defective,
because other sounds are perceived.
Nor is there an absence of other auxiliary causes, because such a thing is unestablished, given that [the cause] possesses positive and negative concomitance.
Nor is it beyond the senses,
because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its conceptualization;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of such conceptualization applying even to things like jars.
Nor is it logical to claim that such a conceptualization [of sound] occurs for the sake of establishing the permanence of sound, because that [position] will be refuted later.

[Ku. 2.218] As for those partial theorists who do not accept this, it is said in reply to them: "The destruction of sound under dispute is perceptible by the senses, because it is an absence perceived by the senses, like the absence of a jar.
To this, they say: "This is not so;
because it is not in contact with the senses, or because its substratum is beyond the senses. If this is argued, we reply: this must be an attempt to point out a limiting condition (*upādhi*).
Or [there might be] a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*) by means of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
It is not the first [case]; regarding the suitability of its own nature (*svarūpayogyatā*), [it is not negated].
Because the capacity for cooperative causation (*sahakāri-yogyatā*) is not a limiting condition (*anupādhi*),
since it remains established at all times in dependence upon that very [capacity];
nor is the perceptibility of absence (*abhāva*) caused by its having a sensory organ as its substratum.
Because it would follow that even the non-existence of phenomena and so forth would likewise possess that same status.
For this very reason, it is not produced by both [causes];
nor is the second [alternative] tenable.
Because the first [reason] is unestablished.
For there exists an innate qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) between the auditory organ and the absence of sound.
Since the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), how can it be the object of a sensory determinate cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*)?
If it is asked, "How can there be the status of a qualifier for one who does not establish the qualified in that way?"— we say no;
because establishing the qualified in that manner is the result [of the qualifier],
but that itself is not what constitutes being a qualifier.

Because it would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*): the apprehension of inherence (*samavāya*) and non-existence (*abhāva*) occurs by way of being qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), and being a qualifier consists precisely in such an apprehension. Therefore, their very nature is indeed to be conjoined with those [substrata] without requiring any further relation.
And that very capacity for producing a qualified cognition is called "qualification" (viśeṣaṇatā);
and this is unavoidable here, because by its very nature, absence [is related] to the locus of its counter-positive.
Because it is already established.

Even so, if it is argued that the cognition must nevertheless be produced by that [means] in that very manner— no, because pervasion (vyāpti) is delimited by the fact that the qualificandum (viśeṣya) is being apprehended.

Otherwise, since it is observed that a cognition of a qualified conceptualization regarding color and so forth arises through the relation of inherence-in-the-conjoined (*saṃyukta-samavāya*), it would follow by implication that the same would apply to odor and so forth as well.
Nevertheless, the perception of anything as a qualifier by way of being a qualifier of the sense organ itself is not observed;
rather, it occurs by way of being a qualifier of that which is connected to the sense organ.
If it is argued that "it (the non-existence) ceases from this [contact]," we say no; for this restriction has as its object that which is related to an object in sensory contact.

Otherwise, since perception of odor and the like is observed through *saṃyuktasamavāya* (inherence in what is conjoined), while perception is not observed through *samavāya* (inherence) alone, it would follow that sound could not be apprehended.
Nor can there be a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*) on the grounds that, even if it were a non-entity (*abhāva*), its substratum is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).
This is because pervasion (vyāpti) is conditioned by the absence of fitness (yogyatā).

Nor is the absence of fitness for that [pervasion] simply its having a supersensible substratum; for that would result in the opposite of that [absence]—namely, the possession of such a substratum—being itself fitness.
Nor is it exactly so, because that would entail the undesirable consequence of perceiving the destruction of dharmas and the like.
If it is argued that its fitness consists in both having a perceptible locus and having a perceptible counter-correlate, we say no— because we do not accept a rule that it must be defined by both.
For absence is indeed defined solely by its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).
Otherwise, even this cognition—"there is no jar on this ground"—would not be perceptual;
for it is conjunction (*saṃyoga*) that is being negated here.
And the absence of that [jar] exists in the jar as well, just as it does in the ground.
In that case, if the ground is useful [as the locus] by virtue of being perceptible,
the same would apply to the jar as well.
Because there is no distinction. If, then, the utility of the jar is of one kind, the utility of the ground must likewise be of another kind, because there is no distinction.
If it is asked, "How else [could this be]?"—[the answer is: for the purpose of defining the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) and for the purpose of the contact (*sannikarṣa*) with the absence.
In that regard, the definition of the counter-positive occurs through recollection even when it is not being perceived;
therefore, for that purpose, the perceptibility of either [the counter-positive or the locus] need not be required.
How could there be contact for both? For the absence of the conjunction between the earth-surface and the jar has no direct contact with the sense organ;
and as for that [medium] by which it exists, if the sense organ were not in contact with that either, [it would not perceive it].

How, indeed, could one cause that [object] to be known? Nor is the sense faculty brought into contact with the object solely by means of what has already been perceived and what is presently being perceived, for that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
Therefore, when there is sensory contact, the ground is also perceived due to its suitability;

however, we consider it logical that its being perceived is not a constituent factor for the perception of absence (*abhāva*). In the present case, however, its utility does not lie in defining the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), because—like conjunction—it cannot be defined by means of a substratum (*ādhāra*).
Nor is it for the sake of proximity,
because the absence of that [object] is directly in sensory contact;
if this were not so, [the following would occur].
From what source does this conviction arise that "the sound previously heard no longer exists"?
If it is argued that it is from inference (*anumāna*), [we reply] no, because the sound itself would have to be made the subject (*pakṣa*) [of that inference]. (80)
Because the reason lacks a substratum;

for when proving mere impermanence, the non-existence [of the reason] is not established as being restricted to a specific time. Furthermore, if space were taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), the reason—"not being perceived as possessing that [impermanence]"—would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Because it exists even at the time when the sound is present;
thus, there is a fault even in the position that [the auditory organ] is the time.

If it is argued: "I am now possessed of an auditory organ devoid of sound, because I lack the perception of sound, like a deaf person"—this is not so, because the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
And because it is contradictory:
to say that one is both deaf and possesses hearing is a contradiction.
Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of that hearing when it is devoid of sound.

If it is argued that the proof [for the non-existence of the final sound] is the futility of the production of something that cannot be experienced, we say no; for its occurrence is possible, just as in the case of the first and subsequent sounds.
If it is argued that those [preceding sounds] have utility toward the commencement of another sound while the final one does not, we say no; for the status of being "final" is unestablished.
Furthermore, because we cannot discern the presence or absence of a purpose for all things that possess an origin,
and because such a purpose is logically established by the example of the function of inhalation and exhalation during the state of deep sleep;
for there is an invariable concomitance (vyāpti) that wherever there is an undertaking, there must necessarily be a purpose.
However, one should not desist from undertaking [the investigation] merely because a purpose is not perceived at first glance;
for if that were the case, the very production of the ear-cavity as a limitation of space would cease for him,
since it would be of no use to a deaf person.
At the time of dispute, the deaf person possesses sound because they occupy a suitable location and their ear-cavity is unobstructed, just like the ear-cavity of others; thus, drums,
lutes, and flutes are not devoid of sound.
Because, while being capable of association with that same cognition, it is perceived even when that [other object] is not perceived;
for whatever is capable of association with that same cognition...

If it is argued that even when that [absence] is not perceived, it is nevertheless perceived as being possessed of its absence— just as one perceives the floor as "devoid of a jar"— we say no, because there is a lack of the capacity for co-occurrence within a single cognition;
for the word [denoting the absence] is based on hearing (is auditory).
Furthermore, because lutes and the like are visible objects.
If it is argued that this is due to mere conceit, even so,
the destruction of sound does not occupy that same location.
And because absolute non-existence is restricted by time.
It might be argued: "Just as sound, the drums and other such things are indeed adjuncts (*upādhi*) of space;
therefore, sound being enjoined with respect to them is in fact enjoined with respect to space itself."

If it is argued that what is being negated becomes negated only within that very locus—just as pleasure and so forth are negated within the body—we say no; for in that case, since the self is established by perception as possessing limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika*), the negation of pleasure and so forth is likewise not established by perception.
But this is not the case here.
This is because the ether conditioned by those [limitations] is not perceptible.
If it is argued that the limitations themselves are indeed perceptible, we say no; for non-existence cannot be defined by them.
Or, if it were so defined, it would follow that it must also be grasped by perception.
This being the case, it is not the fact that non-existence must be defined by means of an ultimate substratum;
nor are those [substrata] established everywhere by perception, since [the object] is perceived even when there is an intervention by the cause of sound.

If it is argued that such linguistic usage occurs because those [non-existents] are inferred from the cognition of the non-existence of the sound, we say no; for the reason— that they are not perceived as possessing that [sound]— is inconclusive,
and because at the time of cognizing the absence, the locus [of the reason] is doubtful.
Furthermore, under the view that the qualificandum is being perceived, [the reason] is unestablished,
because of the intervention of the sense organ and because the word-as-evidence is not perceived.
Furthermore, how is the destruction of substances, qualities, and actions perceived when their substratum has perished?
If you say "in no way at all," then from what source do you derive the principle that "the destruction of the effect follows from the destruction of the substratum"?
If you say it is because such is perceived through inference, we say no; for the answer has already been given by means of an equal logic.

If it is argued that even when the threads have perished, the cloth would not perish and would therefore be perceived in exactly the same way— then let the supporting evidence for this reasoning be stated.

If it is argued that "what is perceived here does not possess a causal series, because while being perceptible, it is not perceived as such"—we say no; for if the probandum is that the constituent parts (the threads) do not have the cloth as their substratum, it results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*).

If the probandum is that they possess the destruction of the cloth, it is contradicted (*bādhitatvāt*), because destruction resides only in the locus of its own counter-positive (the thing destroyed) and its cause.

If it is argued that the thesis to be proven is: "Those threads which possess the destruction of the cloth, these fibers possess its absence," this is not so—because since the destruction of the cloth occurs after the destruction of the threads, it is impossible for the fibers to possess it [the destruction of the cloth].
Furthermore, if one were merely proving a potential capacity, the destruction of the cloth would remain unestablished.
Because its destruction and non-destruction are identical. [Ku.
2.232] If it is argued that—since there is no other possible resort—when a qualified negation is made, the absence of the qualifiers is also understood;

for instance, the cognition arises that "the threads, which are the substratum of the cloth possessing qualities and actions, do not exist in their own parts"—nevertheless, what is the locus of the perceived destruction of the qualities, the actions, and the cloth?
Thus it should be stated.
If you say, "It is only in the case of a horse," then this is an error; for that [horse] does not exist in that location.

If it is argued that, because they [the destructions] are not far removed from those [substrata] by virtue of delimiting their locus, they possess that very location, and thus the determination of the destruction is made by means of such a location— since there is no deviation regarding its fitness— it follows that there is no rule that the determination of destruction must be made solely by means of the location of the substratum of the counter-positive,
for it can be determined in other ways as well.

Therefore, for whatever thing there is a specific collection of conditions for its apprehension, when that collection is present, the absence of that thing must be ascertained in some location or at some time, setting aside those conditions.
However, this is the distinction: if that collection of conditions is indeed present, [then the absence can be established].
If the knower exists even when [the object] is not present through perception,
then it is established that [the knower is known] by means of inference and so forth.
By this, one should understand that the contradiction with such scriptural passages as "non-existence is defined by two existents" is resolved;
for [non-existence] has as its object a counter-positive (pratiyogin) to be defined by both [existence and non-existence], and because it is an object of inference.
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of the unestablished nature of the substratum (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
Even in that case, there is no restriction to the number [of instances];
rather, mere cognition (*jñānamātra*) is what is intended.
Because that much alone is useful for it;
for in some cases, the apprehension [of the substratum] depends upon the convergence of a complete causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
Moreover, if the treatise were intent upon the apprehension of the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*), [it would not have stated this].
One should not cite the example: "The destruction of that [fuel] occurs like the destruction following the destruction of what is to be burned by fire," because it is unestablished (*asiddha*).
For the destruction of fire does not [occur] within the succession of its constituent parts.
It cannot be determined through direct perception because those [causes] cannot be perceived;
nor can it be inferred through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) based on the absence of movement elsewhere and so forth, because the reason (*hetu*) itself cannot be established.
Because the basis [of cognition] is not perceived,
it is also not logical to claim that all this will be established at once through the destruction of the causal signs (*nimitta*);
for that [destruction] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
If it is argued that this is not a fault because [the destruction] is qualified by brilliance (*tejas*), we say no— because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished.
For it is nowhere established that the substance of fire (*tejodravya*) necessarily perishes due to the destruction of its fuel,
since the operation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not admitted [to prove such a case].

Therefore, since it is impossible for [an entity] to go elsewhere by abandoning that [place], one must— even if unwillingly— accept that destruction is defined by that very location, such as the cause and so forth, because there is no other alternative.
For this very reason, even though darkness is perceptible, the teachers maintain that it is a non-entity (*abhāva*).
By this, the prior non-existence of sound (*śabda-prāgabhāva*) is also explained.
This being established, inference is also stated: "Sound is impermanent."
Because it has the nature of arising, like a jar;
nor is this [argument] sublated by recognition,
since that [recognition] is no different from the recognition of a flame and so forth.

If it is argued: "It is not so, because that which is uncontradicted is intrinsically valid (*svataḥ-pramāṇatva*)," then the same applies here. [The opponent replies: "In the case of a flame, that [intrinsic validity] does not exist, because of the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddha-dharmādhyāsa*). (91)
Because it is sublated;
otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total destruction of the conventional usage of difference,
due to the absence of a basis for it.
If it is argued that "if there were randomness (ākasmikatva), there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga)," this is equally applicable;
for even in the case of sound, there exists intensity, greater intensity, dullness, and greater dullness.

If it is argued that these are not inherent (svābhāvika) in that case, we say no; because the principle for determining inherent nature, which has been established in various other instances, applies here as well.

For there is no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) besides direct perception (pratyakṣa) to establish that coldness and fluidity are the inherent natures (svābhāvika) of water, or that heat and luminosity are the inherent natures of fire.
That [which is perceived] is established as being exactly so.

If it is argued that this is because no other limiting condition (*upādhi*) is perceived, and because it is invariably perceived as residing in that [subject], this is equally applicable [to our case].
If it is further argued that there might still be a suspicion that it is a property of something else beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), this too is exactly the same [in its logical status].
Is it then the case that whatever is perceived as being located in something belongs to that very thing?
But if so, then a conch-shell would be yellow.
It would follow that a crystal is red or a cloth is blue [by virtue of proximity], since there is no distinction [between these cases];
but this is not so, because yellowness and the like are established as properties of other things, while conch shells and the like are established as possessing properties contrary to those.
Furthermore, because [the perception of pitch] follows the presence and absence of factors such as the hibiscus flower, and because its erroneous nature is determined by sublation,
there is no establishment here of highness, higher-highness, and so forth as properties belonging to something else;
nor is there a state of contradictory properties among the letter-sounds "ga" produced by parrots, starlings, and the like.
Nor does it follow the positive and negative concomitance of any other subject possessing that property.
If it is argued that a doubt might still arise despite this, [we reply: this would apply everywhere in such a case;
and thus, [the certainty] would not exist anywhere at all. (93)
For someone, something might be established from somewhere;
yet this cannot even be suspected.

Because there is an absence of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) regarding what is not previously perceived, and because it is impossible to superimpose [a property] upon that which has not been brought forward by mental impressions;
nor are the properties of sound itself being apprehended.

Since the skin and other sense organs do not function with respect to entities that are not included within [the objects of] touch and so forth, nor is there apprehension of them by hearing alone; for, like the eye, hearing—being non-material (avāyavīya)—cannot grasp the qualities of air.
Furthermore, properties such as "high" or "higher-pitched" are not qualities of air, because they are audible, just like the phonemes *ka* and so forth.
Or else, sound does not have the property of being perceivable by hearing because it possesses form, like the earth;
and if this were not the case,
it would follow that the phonemes beginning with 'ka' are also composed of air.
What follows from this? If it were a quality of a composite whole, it would be impermanent;
if it were a quality of an atom, it would be unperceivable. Both of these [consequences] are undesirable for you.
And hearing must necessarily possess qualities of a nature capable of being grasped, because it is an external sense organ, like the olfactory sense and so forth.
Let it be that sounds are also not mere appearances.

If it is argued that the apprehension of its properties would thus be possible through the ear, we say no; for in the perception "this *ga*-sound is loud" or "very loud," the articulations (*dhvani*) themselves do not manifest.
Furthermore, there can be no manifestation of a universal (*sāmānya*) without the manifestation of the individual (*vyakti*), because of the absence of a cause;
for the causal complex for the manifestation of the universal is necessarily included within the causal complex for the manifestation of the individual.
Whence is this known? From the understanding of it through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka);
for the apprehension of the universal occurs only in respect to perceptible objects such as jars and the like.
Furthermore, since there is no apprehension of the mind and other internal organs— which transcend the senses—
their own essential fitness (*svarūpayogyatā*) alone must be the cause in those cases;

if it is argued that the fitness of the individual manifestation (*vyaktiyogyatā*) is not the cause, then, by the same logic, since existence (*sattā*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), earthiness (*pārthivatva*), and so forth possess their own essential fitness, it would follow that they should be perceived even in atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the like.
If there were an incapacity [to perceive], then it would follow that even jars and other such objects could not be perceived; this is an insurmountable predicament.

Therefore, the capacity to perceive a universal is necessarily included within the capacity to perceive the individual; thus, when that [individual] is not perceived, the universal itself is simply not perceived.

Consequently, since there is no possibility of superimposing properties such as "high-pitchedness" [onto a sound], and since its inherent nature is established, the distinction [between sounds] is ultimately real due to the imposition of contradictory attributes. Thus, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
There is no sublation by that [reason],
nor is there a case of counter-balanced opposition (satpratipakṣatva);
for two things that are mutually contradictory cannot possess actual equal strength.

When considering the deficiency of one or another of the [required] factors, if there is such a deficiency, it is that very factor which must be stated [as missing]; whereas if there is no deficiency, it must follow that [the opponent's position] itself is deficient. Thus, that which is inferior cannot serve as a valid counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*).
Nevertheless, [the opponent claims]: "Sound is eternal."

If it is argued that even here, because sound is not a substance (*adravya*), something must be stated regarding its status as a substance during the stage of proof—[we reply: that is unestablished (*asiddhi*).
If it is argued that sound is established as a substance because it is perceived through a direct relation (*sākṣātsambandha*), like a jar—no; for this too is unestablished.

Indeed, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the direct relation of sound so long as its being a quality of the auditory organ (*śrotra-guṇatva*) or its being a substance remains unestablished.
“If there remains [something], namely:

since the three categories beginning with *sāmānya* are excluded by their non-difference from *sat* (existence) and so forth, and since *karmatva* (action-ness) is excluded by the negation of inherence in a corporeal substance, there remains either substance-ness (*dravyatva*) or quality-ness (*guṇatva*); thus, one of the two relations—conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*)—must apply,” if this is argued, it is not so, due to the force of subverting evidence (*bādhaka*).

Furthermore, because substance-ness (*dravyatva*) would also be excluded by the remainder [of the categories], there would arise the fault of contradicting the means of valid cognition that apprehends the gender [of the term].

Alternatively, if substance-ness were not excluded despite the presence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), it would follow that action-ness (*karmatva*) and the other categories would likewise not be excluded; thus, the "remainder" of the other [categories] would remain unestablished.
Therefore, the "remainder of one part" (*ekadeśapariśeṣa*) is not a valid means of proof.
Because it is merely the cause for the contraction of doubt.
Now, what is the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against its being a substance (*dravya*)?
It is said: Sound is not a substance, because it is the cause for the determination of external sense-faculties, like color and so forth.

Thus, by the method of elimination, once its status as a quality (*guṇa*) is established through the proof of its inherence (*samavāya*), the establishment of its substantiality (*dravyatva*)— on the grounds that it is perceivable through an immediate relation— is refuted by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the inferential mark (*liṅga*).
Nor can there be a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) based on what is unestablished (*asiddha*), because that which is unestablished possesses inferior strength.
Now, as for sound... [97]
That it is not a quality of the auditory faculty has been established by you yourself through a continuous argument.
Nor is it a quality of the auditory faculty,
because it is perceived by that [faculty].
That which is perceived by a particular sense organ is not a quality of that organ, just as odor and so forth, though they are perceived, are not qualities of the sense organs.
If it is argued that the ear does not perceive its own quality because it is a sense organ, like the nose, and thus the existence of a quality [in sound] is not established— what follows from this?
This too is not [conclusive],
because the fact that the nose and other organs do not perceive the odors and so forth inherent in themselves is not a sufficient reason to prove that [sound] is their own quality.
(98) For in that case, "unfitness" (*ayogyatva*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*).
Otherwise: pleasure and so forth are not qualities of the self, because they are perceived by it, like color and so forth;
or else, they are not perceived by it, because they are inherent in it, like unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
One might also suspect that the self is not the grasper of that [pleasure], because it is its substratum, just as a jar, which is the substratum of odor and so forth, is not.
Therefore, whether it be one's own quality or another's quality, what is unfit is not perceived;
however, what is fit is perceived, and what is unfit is not.
What, then, is untenable here?
[Verse 2.248] Furthermore, the auditory organ must necessarily be a grasper of its own specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa), because it is a sense faculty;
otherwise, its creation would be purposeless.
(99) Because that which is other than it is apprehended by another sense-organ alone,
and there is no utility for it in the apprehension of a specific substance;
(100) because a sense-organ grasps a substance only by relying on the suitability of its specific quality.
It is not by mere suitability of the substance's own nature [that something is perceived];
otherwise, since lunar light is suitable by its own nature, it too would be perceived;
or else, since the self or the mind would be graspable, they would be perceived even in the state of deep sleep.
Or rather, the eye functions even with respect to a color that is unmanifest.
Therefore, it is an established principle that the sense organs apprehend a substance only by taking into account the suitability of its qualities, and not otherwise.
For this very reason, space and the other [elements] are not visible to the eye.
Let it be then that sound is eternal, because it is a unique quality of the eternal space, like its [quality of] supreme magnitude.
If it is argued that there is a counter-inference (pratyanumāna) stating "it possesses magnitude," we say no; for the limiting condition (upādhi) of "not being an effect" is present.

Otherwise, one could likewise argue: "The specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa) of the self are eternal, because they are qualities unique to that [self], just like the extreme largeness (paramamahattva) residing therein."

If it is argued that this [reason] is not a valid reason because it is sublated by perception (*pratyakṣabādhitatva*), we say no; for there is no possibility of sublation in the case of a [reason] that is free from adventitious conditions (*nirupādhi*).
Furthermore, if that which is essentially connected [to the probandum] were to abandon it, it would follow that its very nature is abandoned.
Therefore, it is by means of sublation that an adventitious condition is inferred.
Or otherwise—there is no distinction whatsoever.
By this, the argument "because it is audible, like the nature of sound (śabdatva)" is also refuted; for here too, that very same thing serves as the limiting adjunct (upādhi).
Otherwise, it would follow that odor, color, taste, and touch are also eternal;

for one could easily formulate the following argument: "They are eternal because they are each perceivable by a single sense organ, such as the nose, just like the quality of odor (gandhatva)," and so forth.
Since contradiction and deviation are impossible here, only the fallacy of the unestablished reason (asiddhi) remains. (103)
That [intrinsic nature] also does not exist;
for instance, sound is perceived to possess degrees of excellence and deficiency through its inherent states of intensity, mildness, and so forth, according to the reasoning previously stated.
Moreover, this possession of excellence and deficiency is observed everywhere as following upon the distinction of causes;
for indeed, those things which are causeless and eternal, such as space and so forth, are invariably possessed of excellence alone.
Or they may be inferior,
such as atoms and the like; however,
nothing that possesses excellence is ever diminished by anything else.

This [property], being excluded from eternal things and existing among those that possess causes, finds its rest only by taking up the state of being produced; thus, it is employed to establish the necessary connection: "Sound is produced, because it is subject to degrees of excellence and deficiency, like sweetness and the like."
Otherwise, if it were to occur without a restricting factor, it would apply even to eternal things (it would occur even in the case of the eternal), because there would be no cause for restriction.

If you argue that this principle applies elsewhere than to sound, we say no; for an objection could be raised against every inference with equal ease, namely, that it excludes the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*).
Moreover, in this case, there can be no variation in the degree of manifestation based on a variation in the degree of the manifestor,
for that would entail the consequence that [the manifested nature] is not intrinsic;
and yet, its intrinsic nature is established.
Furthermore, there is no conformity to anything other than the manifestor and the producer;
nor is any mode other than being intrinsic (svābhāvika) or adventitious (aupādhika) possible. [Ku. 2.252] It might be argued as follows:
Even so, what contradiction is there between arising and permanence,
such that a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) could be established?
And since that [connection] is not established, [your argument fails].

If it is argued: "For you, this reason is unestablished as being pervasive; for us, it is irrelevant; and for the Buddhists, it is a reason whose exclusion from the counter-example is doubtful"—we say no.

For this quality of having an origin, upon the exclusion of eternal things—which are incompatible with the proximity of a cause of destruction—ceases to exist when its own pervader [existence] is withdrawn, and thus it rests in that which is perishable and possesses the proximity of a cause of destruction.

If it is asked: "How is it determined that 'that which necessarily arises must do so through the proximity of a cause of destruction'? The answer is: No, for its non-proximity does not occur due to an intrinsic contradiction of nature, as is the case with space (*ākāśa*) and the like; rather, it is because of the contradiction between arising and [the absence of] a cause of destruction.
Because their coexistence is observed.
As for the non-proximity of two things that are not contradictory, it would be due to spatial distance, as in the case of the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains.
Furthermore, the distance between two locations must be due either to contradiction or to the absence of a cause [for proximity].
For the reasons stated previously, the first [alternative] is not tenable;
as for the second, it would be like the case of a cloth and saffron:
if the cloth were to perish immediately upon contact with the destroyer, just as the cloth perishes immediately upon contact with saffron.
For just as there is no destruction without a cause of destruction,
so too, if it were the case that there is no destruction of the cloth without its contact with saffron, who could prevent their conjunction?

Therefore, the non-association of two non-contradictory things is pervaded by the rule of temporal distance. Since that [temporal distance] is excluded from this [case], it excludes its own pervader; thus, the logical connection (*pratibandha*) is established.
This might be so.
If it is asked, "If the word is thus non-eternal,
how can its connection with the meaning be apprehended?"— [the answer is: just as [the connection] of a non-eternal object [is apprehended] by that [word],
so too is the universal (*jāti*) alone the referent of the word (*padārtha*).
If it is argued that the individual (vyakti) is not [denoted], we say no—because it would follow that the individual could not be obtained from the word.
If it is argued that it is obtained through implication (ākṣepa), then what indeed is this so-called "implication"? It is, first of all, inference (anumāna).

If it is argued that because it is impossible to grasp the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) even with respect to its association with infinite [individuals], or alternatively, if it were possible, then association itself would be just as easily grasped, and thus the inseparable relation exists merely in the form of the individuals themselves— this is not so, because there is no universal (*sāmānya*) called "individuality" (*vyaktitva*).
Or, even if it exists, since it does not imply its specific particulars even when it implies that [general category],
let its expressibility also be exactly like that;
what is the use of implication?
"Because there is no contradiction with the logical connection" (saṅgati).
If it is argued that "presumption (arthāpatti) is implication (ākṣepa)," we say no—what is unaccounted for without the manifestation of the individual (vyakti)?
If it is argued that it is the "universal" (jāti), we say no—because it exists even in the states of its destruction or non-arising.
“If you say, ‘Even so, [the cognition of the universal] does not occur without the individual,’ we say no—because the word ‘mere’ (mātra) has no meaning here.
If you say, ‘The cognition of the universal is impossible without the cognition of the individual,’ we say no—because it arises even in the absence of that [cognition].
[If you argue that] the individual is the object...”

If it is argued that its [the universal's] being the object of that [cognition] is untenable without [it having] the genus as its object, we say no; for if that is so, then what is untenable about their being the domain of a single cognition,
and what would it [the universal] be made to convey?
If it is argued that "the individual is determined through the impossibility of the continuity of the genus," we say no, because this would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*).

It might be thought: even without an invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*), a logical mark (*liṅga*) reaches its conclusion regarding a particular by the force of its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
If it is argued that, even in the absence of syntactic connection (*saṅgati*), a word reaches its specific meaning through a particular power (*śaktiviśeṣa*),
and that this very process is called "implication" (*ākṣepa*)— we reply: first of all, comprehension does not occur sequentially,
because in the absence of anything further to be expected, a repeated operation (*viramyavyāpāra*) is impossible.
If it is argued that [the cognition of] the universal depends on the communication [of the individual], then enough with the postulation of a distinct power of the word;
for its establishment is achieved by that alone.
If it is replied "yes," we say no—because it has already been stated that a cognition of the universal is impossible if it does not have an individual as its objective support.
Furthermore, it would entail the undesirable consequence of [the cognition] falling under another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*).
If it is argued that this is not a fault because "that" is a memory, we say no—because it would entail the consequence that there is no connection with what has not been previously experienced.
If it is argued that let there be only a single cognition, then enough with the postulation of two distinct powers (*śakti*).

And thus, just as the single power whose object is the universal culminates in that which possesses it (the individual), so too the connection whose locus is the universal would culminate in that which possesses it.
Furthermore, even though phonemes are eternal, they do not connect with word-meanings when deprived of their specific accents, sequences, and so forth.
Nor is their being qualified by that [universal] eternal;
therefore, it is only those objects and words that are situated within the scope of their respective universals that are connected,
and not otherwise.
One should not even suspect that the eternity of the word (śabda) follows from this;

for when even the phonemes (varṇa) themselves are not eternal, what then can be said of words, which consist of collections of phonemes characterized by sequences and so forth dependent upon a person's intention to speak?
How much less, then, could there be such a thing as a sentence, whose nature consists in a specific arrangement of that collection? And how much less still,
the Veda, which is a collection of those [sentences]?
If it is argued that we define permanence as the non-interruption of the stream due to the successive dependence of dependent persons upon one another— this too is not the case,
because of the possibility of creation and dissolution.

Because a day-and-night must necessarily be preceded by a [prior] day-and-night; because it is impossible for the activity [of karmas] to cease simultaneously due to their having unequal times of ripening;
and because the systematic arrangement of the social classes (*varṇa*) and so forth would be untenable.
Because if conventions were not apprehended (or were impossible), it would follow that linguistic usage would be abolished,
as in the case of "pot" (or "cloth").

If it is asked, "How can this be so, lest there be the consequence of breaking the tradition?"—it is said: The obstruction of [worldly] activity is a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of existence, like the rainy season and so forth; it is like deep sleep.
The castes (*varṇas*) are like [the appearance of] a scorpion from within a fruit; the conventions (*samayas*) and so forth are like *māyā*. (2)

Because proving merely that it is preceded by that [previous cognition] results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*), and because being immediately preceded by that is not a necessary condition (*aprayojakatvāt*);
for this is logically consistent with the breakdown of the rule that a specific day is preceded by the days of the rainy season and so forth.
For that [distinction] is indeed caused by the temporal adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the specific conjunction with the zodiac signs and so forth;
for it ceases precisely upon the absence of those [conjunctions].
Likewise here too, [the distinction] is dependent on the temporal adjunct consisting of the duration of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), which is the cause for the persistence of the creation.
Since that [property] belongs to it, what fault is there in its very absence being the exclusion?
Nor is it unproduced or imperishable,
because it possesses parts.
[Ku. 2.260] For the cessation of mental activity is also possible in the state of deep sleep;
indeed, it is not the case that "actions whose time of ripening is indefinite" become entirely averse to experience at that time.
For there can be no such thing as experience for one who is not conscious, because of the contradiction.
What, then, is the purpose of the body at that time? It serves no purpose whatsoever with respect to it. If so, for what reason does it persist?
For the sake of future enjoyment,
as in the case of the eye and so forth.
For what purpose does it breathe?
It is for the purpose of distinguishing the states of the lifespan through the continuity of inhalation and exhalation; for by means of that,
a specific experience is established.

If it is argued that this is somehow possible for a single individual but not for the whole world— [we reply: because of the infinity of karmas, the indeterminacy of the time of their ripening, and the nature of karmas as both the oppressor and the oppressed,
[this applies] to the whole world.
Or what distinction is there for one [person] such that it would not happen to him,
yet deep sleep occurs for everyone? (112)
If it is argued that [the destruction] occurs sequentially and not simultaneously, we say no; for the sequence of effects depends upon the sequence of causes.
Nor must the causes, having arrived by the power of their own conditions, necessarily act only in a sequential manner;
for there is no fixed rule, just as in the case of a total eclipse (sarvagrāsa).

For even though there is no fixed rule for the conjunction of the planets at other times, it might nonetheless happen at some point— just as a total eclipse of all the lunar mansions might occur despite the lack of a fixed rule regarding the digits [of the moon] and so forth— or like the simultaneous gathering of the three humors (tridoṣa).

For just as there may at one time be a *sannipāta* (conjunction) of wind, bile, and phlegm despite the lack of a fixed order for their accumulation, aggravation, and subsidence— and this results in the destruction of the body— so too,

when there is a *sannipāta* of the fire of time, the wind, and the great ocean during the state of the dissolution of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), what contradiction is there in the fact that conscious beings would simultaneously become devoid of experience?
If it is argued that it is nonetheless difficult to maintain that the Videhas are performers of ritual action (*karmin*), what here is so difficult?
For this is possible precisely because of the cessation of the body, the senses, and the objects—which serve as the causes [of action]—just as there is a cessation of experience.
Furthermore, the established order of castes and stages of life is also possible, just as in the case of the letters *ka* and so forth.

For just as, although a scorpion is preceded by a scorpion, its first instance arises from cow dung; and although a taṇḍulīyaka plant is preceded by a taṇḍulīyaka plant, [its first instance arises from something else].
The first [instance] is from a grain of rice and so forth;
even though fire is preceded by fire, the first instance is from the fire-drill wood.
In this way, milk, curd, clarified butter, oil, plantain stalks, and so forth— even though they are preceded by humans, animals, cows, or Brahmins—
their initial states are caused solely by specific types of elements bound to their respective actions.

Since that very cause is pervasive everywhere, what is inconsistent about the fact that all those belonging to that continuum possess the same generic nature (*sāmānyajātīyatva*)? If you say, "In that case, [the inference] beginning with 'this is preceded by a cow because it possesses cowness' (*gotvāt*) has already been refuted," we reply: it has not been refuted, because that was established only with respect to those born from a womb (*yonija*).

"But mental [effects] may arise otherwise. If it is argued: "Why could something not happen now as well, just as in the case of dung-scorpions and the like? We say no—because specific effects are restricted to specific times.
For a lotus-shoot does not arise from cow dung during the rainy season; would it then arise in winter? (Or would it not? No, it would not.
Even the convention is established by a single person alone,
like a magician;
it is easily accomplished through conventional usage itself, based on various effects situated in the relationship between the one to be instructed and the instructor.
For just as a magician employs a wooden puppet, empowered by the movement of strings,
saying, "Bring this," and that wooden puppet does exactly so; so it is here.
Just as a child is instructed regarding that [perception] by means of the conventional usage of "volition" (*cetanā*) and so forth, so too should it be here;
for even the understanding of action arises from those very [examples], such as potters and weavers.

[Ku. 2.264] If it is asked what the proof is for the very beginning of creation, [the answer is]: this continuum of the universe was initiated by inherent causes that were devoid of a perceptible continuum, because it is a continuum, like the continuum of fire produced from two pieces of wood (araṇi).

Furthermore, the atoms of the present Brahmāṇḍa must have previously produced another continuum of the same kind, because, while being eternal, they are initiators of such [a continuum], like the atoms of a lamp-flame, and so forth.
Moreover, both production and destruction would [otherwise] be impossible.
If it is argued that there is no contradiction in the non-interruption of the continuum, we say no— for in that case,
there would likewise be a non-interruption of the continuum of jars and other such things.

But the opposite is observed. If it is argued that this [activity] is prompted by the production of specific enjoyments such as a body (or agent), etc., we say no— because that is absent in the case of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*).
And likewise, in that case, if there were no removal of its parts, it would follow that it is beginningless, which would contradict its being a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).
Therefore, whatever effect exists, its persistence is dependent upon something else.
Upon the removal of that [cause], there is the cessation of that [effect];
whatever has a certain cause, upon the presence of that cause, there is the arising of that effect.
Nor is the basis for the persistence of an effect something eternal,
because that would entail its eternal persistence;
nor is the cause itself eternal.
Because it would otherwise follow that [the result] is not occasional.
Therefore, this matter is entirely free from waves [of doubt].
And in such a state of affairs, experience (*bhoga*) must likewise be brought about by *karmas* without overstepping the very nature of things.

Thus, just as in the case of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), this same principle applies to the entire universe, from the egg of an ant up to the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*); such is the establishment of the logical connection (*pratibandhasiddhi*).
And so, if the cosmic egg were to originate from atoms, and if those atoms were independent and remained separate, where then would the hosts of living beings contained within it abide?
It is like a swarm of gnats within an udumbara fruit inside the cheek of an enraged monkey;
or like a multitude of wood-boring insects reeling within the heart of timber being consumed by a forest fire;
or like a caravan of sea-faring merchants whose ship has been cast down by the submarine fire fanned by the winds of universal destruction.
Furthermore: "Moreover, let the decline of the tradition be inferred from the observed decline in birth, purificatory rites, knowledge, capacity, and the practice of Vedic study. (3)
For previously, beings were born of pride;
thereafter, they came into existence through sexual union, with offspring as their sole purpose;
and after that, [they were born] from desire.
They are born from proximity to things to be avoided; nowadays, due to the conditions of place, time, and so forth, they arise for the most part from animal-like behavior alone.
Formerly, however, they were [produced] through ritual refinements such as the *caru* oblation and others. (121)
They were composed;
then [the rites] beginning with the field;
then beginning from the conception.
But now, since [the Vedas] have been produced, one has studied the Veda with its thousand branches by relying on worldly convention (lokavyavahāra).
Then it was divided;
then there was one [school] with six limbs;
but now, however, in some places there is only a single branch.
(122) Formerly, the Brahmins shone forth as those whose livelihood was truth; then, those whose livelihood was untruth;
(123) then, those whose livelihood was death.
At present, most people follow the livelihoods of gambling, falsehood, usury, cattle-rearing, and the service of dogs.
Formerly, guests were obtained by the Brahmins only with great difficulty.
Then they became guests of the kṣatriyas; after that, they even entered among the vaiśyas; and now they have become eaters of the food of śūdras as well.
After that, those who eat remnants; after that, those who eat food;
now, however, are those who eat only sin.
Formerly, the Dharma had four quarters; then, as austerity waned, it became three-quartered;
then, as knowledge declined, it became two-quartered.

At present, the sacrifice decays; its single remaining foot, "giving," is rendered unstable by hundreds of ailments such as ill-gotten gains, stained by the impurity of lack of faith, and shattered by hundreds of thorns such as desire and anger. Because its strength diminishes day by day, it is perceived as if stumbling here and there.

If it is argued that "just as now, so too everywhere, nothing more than what is seen in the examples is required," we say no; for we observe the disappearance of those Vedic branches (*śākhā*) whose existence was inferred from the practice of the Smṛtis.
Furthermore, the authority of the Smṛtis and of custom is not accepted as independent, and there is a lack of evidence for Manu and others having perceived supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārtha*).

If one accepts that tradition (smṛti) arises from practice (ācāra) and practice arises from tradition, then by admitting such beginninglessness, there follows the fallacy of a "blind succession" (andhaparaṃparā).
Furthermore, since that which has not been recited throughout the cycle of saṃsāra cannot be considered the Veda, inference regarding its validity is impossible.
Because a mere sequence of syllables, whether considered in terms of its production, its manifestation, or its intended meaning, is devoid of significance;
and if it is inferred that this [Vedic injunction] is a means to achieve one's welfare or is something to be performed because it is the practice of the learned (śiṣṭa).
What is the use of inferring the Veda?
For its meaning is established through inference itself.
Nor can it be argued that because it is the cognition of dharma, this very [inference] is the Veda to be inferred.
Because it is established by direct perception and because it is not based on scripture.

If it is argued that this [practice] is rooted in a means of valid cognition because it is the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), then that results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Because it is accepted that [the Veda] has perception as its basis, and because inference is possible even when that [perception] is absent.
If it is argued: "Since it is eternally unknown, how can it be non-informative, and how can it be an inference or a basis? [We reply: Is the Veda informative while remaining unknown?
Or rather, the root [of inference] is simply that which does not itself convey [the object];
for this reason you hold it to be the most insentient.
If you argue that it must be known because it is inferred, then let the inferential mark (liṅga) be exactly the same.

If it is argued that the cognition of the logical mark (*liṅga*) prior to the cognition of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) is required because it is the cause, whereas a subsequent cognition is not— then the same applies to the cognition of the word (*śabda*).

If it is argued that the fact of being rooted in verbal testimony (*śabdamūlatva*) is inferred from the very nature of established practice (*ācāra*), and that the obligation to act (*kartavyatā*) is understood through that verbal testimony—this is not so; for since the nature of established practice is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it does not depend on any other source.
Therefore, because there is no perception of the obligation to act [in the practice itself], [the inference fails].
Furthermore, because [the Veda] is not cognized, there is no scope for inference from words,
nor is direct perception of the scripture possible;
rather, having inferred the duty [to perform a rite] solely by way of the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra), one infers the underlying word [of the Veda] on that basis.
And so, what is the use of that? For its object has already been established.
Even so, its basis remains nothing other than scripture.
If it is argued that this is because of pervasion (*vyāpti*), then for that very reason, one must infer that its foundation lies in perception and inference.
If it is argued that while [the world] would have a beginning, this [tradition] is beginningless—[we reply that] the practice (*ācāra*) as well... (130)
In that case, this [specific instance] would be the very first of its kind,
whereas this [general principle] would be beginningless even without scripture.
Let there be such beginninglessness for both the performance of conduct and the inference [of it].
If it is asked, "What is lost for us?"—first, the claim that "the Veda is eternally inferable," and second, the claim that "instruction alone is the authority regarding Dharma" [Ku.
2.274]. Now, the underlying intention here is this: even Vedic practices, such as the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices, are seen to be undergoing total extinction.
For these [rites] are not performed now,

yet it is not the case that they were never performed even previously; otherwise, it would follow that the entire body of the Veda, whose purpose is those rites, lacks authority, like an instruction on crossing the ocean [when one has already reached the shore].
And let it not be thus,
because [this view] shares the same logical status as the instruction regarding the New Moon sacrifice and other rituals.
In this way, moreover, there will be some time [in the future].
Where these shall be practiced,
likewise other customs as well shall be abolished and [others] shall be practiced.
Thus, there is no interruption [in the tradition].

If it is argued that, for that reason, [the practice] is rooted in scripture (*āgama*)—then in that case, since there would be no inference of either the duty (*kartavyatva*) or the scripture in the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*) at the beginning of the stream [of tradition], and since there is no direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣaśruti*), how could even the discussion of conduct (*ācārasaṅkathā*) exist? Thus, everything would collapse.
Therefore, direct Vedic revelation alone is the root of traditional practice;
if that no longer exists now, it follows that the Vedic branches have been lost.
If it is argued that it still exists elsewhere even today—then why does it not exist here?
Is it because the lineages of the preceptors have departed elsewhere, or because those very lineages have been extinguished, or rather because of the interruption of the study of the Vedas?
It cannot be the first or the second [alternative];
for if all [people] were to go elsewhere or perish, there would necessarily follow the extinction of the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) in Bhāratavarṣa,
since that [conduct] has the same agent as its learners.
If the practice of study were to occur through the introduction of conduct by those who have come from elsewhere, that might be possible;
however, the third case is not tenable, because such a thing would be impossible as long as there is no interruption of disciples endowed with internal spiritual power.

Therefore, because the capacity for longevity, health, strength, vigor, faith, tranquility, self-restraint, comprehension, and retention diminishes day by day, while the practice of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) is being eroded, we consider it logical that these two somehow persist; furthermore, due to the universal adherence [to tradition], the total destruction of everything does not occur all at once. [Ku. 2.276] (134) Since "the world follows what has gone before," such a practice is indeed devoid of authoritative basis.

If it is argued that there is no destruction of the Vedic branches (*śākhoccheda*), because since the procedural details (*itikartavyatā*) must be supplied from multiple branches, there would be the undesirable consequence of a lack of confidence even regarding a single ritual action— [we reply: No, for in this way, the very acceptance of the tradition by the great community (*mahājanaparigraha*) would be subject to subversion.
If the Vedas too were accepted by people merely out of blind conformity (*gatānugatikatayā*),
they would not be authoritative;
thus, it would be like one fleeing from the fear of a scorpion falling into the mouth of a venomous snake.
Furthermore, the great seers, apprehending the lack of confidence that would arise from the eventual destruction of the Śākya lineage in the course of time, provided a remedy;
therefore, even the aforementioned fault does not apply.
And this destruction does not occur through a sequence of knowledge,
by which it might be praiseworthy;
rather, it occurs through the sequence of the ripening of negligence, intoxication, pride, indolence, and nihilism.
(138) Then, after the end of the interruption, there is again a stream, and immediately after that, once more an interruption; thus it is like the current of the Sarasvatī river;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the loss of what has been done (*kṛtahāna*).
And thus, even though this [manifestation] occurs like a future stream, it is inferred to be preceded by cessation.
And the Blessed Vyāsa records the word of the Blessed One in the Gītā: "Whenever there is a decline of dharma, O Bhārata, and a rise of adharma, then I manifest Myself."
For the protection of the virtuous, for the destruction of the wicked,
and for the sake of establishing righteousness, I manifest myself age after age.
Thus it is said in the *Gītā* (4.7–8). [Ku.
2.278] But what is this "acceptance by the great multitude"?
It is the acceptance, retention, and practice of the meaning [of a teaching] by those who are devoid of the perception of a [logical] reason.
For he would not exist here without a cause;
for in this case, laziness and the like are not the cause, because [the world] is primarily characterized by karma consisting of suffering.
Nor is there entry into this [system] out of necessity, due to a lack of qualification for other means whose validity has been established;
for even those honored by others do not enter here. Nor is it out of passion for the non-duality of food, drink, and so forth.
This is because its purpose is the systematic determination of those divisions;
nor is there any delusion caused by the assault of fallacious reasoning, for it has been practiced since childhood.
Nor is there association with heretics whose speech may be deceptive,
because [the practice] proceeds through the lineage of one's father and so forth;
nor is there an intention toward non-distraction based on the conceit of practicing yoga.
Because the beginner is exceedingly preoccupied with the ritual section (or indeed the ritual section alone),
nor is it for the sake of livelihood.
This is because, according to the reasoning previously stated, there is an absence of visible results;
nor is it a case of deception by trickery,
as that is impossible in the present context.

[2.280] However, these reasons are possible for the acceptance of the scriptures of the Buddhists and others: for instance, "there is greater lightness of ritual action there" appeals to the indolent; "there is admission even for those fallen from this [path]" appeals to those with no other resort; "there is no restriction regarding food and so forth" appeals to the passionate; and "according to one's own will"— [The sentence continues:]—appeals to those who desire autonomy. Thus, these are the reasons for their adherence.

"Seizers" refers to those who practice fallacious reasoning; "those associated with heretics" refers to those who claim that activity [proceeds] due to the absence of a lineage from father and so forth; "those conceited about being undistracted" refers to those who cite such scriptural passages as, "Having understood the difference between the two, for whom is purity prescribed?"; "the unfit" refers to those for whom livelihood consists of eating seven times a day and so forth, [claiming] the paralyzing of the sun and the splitting of stones.
The breaking of branches,
possession by spirits,
and the speaking of images.

Regarding the phrase "alchemical doctrine" and so forth, it is conceivable that they embrace those who have been deceived by tricksters through such means as [the practice of] *dhātuvāda* (which, due to its deceptive nature, is a form of delusion). (144)
Therefore, the distinction is that they are not embraced by the great multitude.
It might be argued: "If this were so, there would be a contradiction in the functioning of all actions, and nothing at all would arise."

Since nothing perishes, in a world resembling still, motionless space, from what specific cause could there be a new creation? The Sāṅkhyas find elegance in the theory of the transformation of *prakṛti*;
the followers of the Bhāskara school find it appropriate to say it is the transformation of *brahman*.
The claim that it is "due to the ripening of latent impressions" (vāsanāparipākāt) follows the Buddhist doctrine.

Furthermore, the claim that it is "due to a specific time" (kālaviśeṣāt) is untenable because there is no specific limiting condition (upādhi). Moreover, non-existent qualifiers cannot function as differentiators at all times.
Because they possess an identical form;
nor by means of cognition,
since that [cognition], being impermanent, is absent at that time.
