If it is argued that this is because there is no distinction in an eternal entity, whether in terms of its objects or its own nature—[we reply: No. Just as for living beings who have fallen asleep due to the exhaustion caused by physical agitation, there continues a stream of breaths whose sole purpose is to bring about the sequential ripening of their lifespan; so too, for atoms which have acquired latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) through the agitation of the dissolution of the great elements, there exists a process culminating in the conjunction known as "accumulation" (*pracaya*), whose sole purpose is to delimit time through degrees of intensity such as slow, slower, and very slow.
Because the continuum of karma proceeds as the breath of Īśvara,
as to how long this [continuum] lasts, it is accepted that it continues for exactly that duration, without contradiction and without overstepping what is established by scripture.
Alternatively, the activity within other cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) serves as the limiting adjunct for time;
when time is delimited by that [activity], creation occurs once again,
just as fruits are spread out upon a pumpkin vine.
Likewise, it is heard in scripture that thousands of cosmic eggs (*aṇḍa*) are pervaded by the power of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).
(145) Such being the case, when separation is possible, whose [Veda] would be accepted by whom, such that its authority might be established?
Furthermore, this object is an indicator (*jñāpaka*), not a causal factor (*kāraka*).
Therefore, since the effect would cease to exist due to the absence of its cause, how could that which is intended to be an indicator establish it?
[Ku. 2.284] It might be argued as follows—(146):

[Objection: There are indeed those such as Kapila and others who have directly realized *dharma* and attained perfection through the yoga of action (*karmayoga*). Seeing living beings being scorched by the embers of *saṃsāra*, they, being supremely compassionate, will favor them with teachings that are both pleasing and beneficial; what is the use of a Supreme Lord who possesses knowledge of the number of insects and other creatures without any [practical] purpose? [Reply: No, because [the Lord is] other than them.
Because there is no confidence in its maturation.
For instance, even if one accepts that meditation is the means for perceiving supersensuous objects, it does not necessarily produce a truly real direct realization— that is,
one in which we can place our trust.

If it is argued that [the validity of the teaching] follows from its corroboration by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), we say no— because in the case of [the rule] "non-violence and so forth are the means to achieve one's welfare," such corroboration is absent.

If it is argued that there exists scripture (*āgama*) [to support it], we say no— because since that too is rooted merely in mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it is likewise a matter regarding which one cannot place full confidence.
If it is argued that activity occurs even through partial correspondence, we say no;
for it is possible otherwise, as in the case of a dream narrative.
Furthermore, there can be no cultivation (*bhāvanā*) with respect to what has not been perceived.
For thieves, snakes, and the like are indeed only imagined as such by those who are fearful.
Furthermore, the fact that ritual action (*karman*) and yoga are means for achieving one's welfare has not been perceived from any source; nor is it... [ta]... perceived.
The perception of its own nature (svarūpa) is not useful anywhere,
nor is it something to be accomplished through cultivation (bhāvanā);
furthermore, positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) are not possible in this case.
Because the fruit is suitable for another body, it is not perceived [in this life]; therefore, there is no performance of it [in this life]. (149)
And because that [self] does not exist,
it is not the case that [the continuity of action and result] is established merely through the linking of two bodies— one as the agent and the other as the enjoyer;
for that [linking] is absent.
For no one connects [the two moments], thinking, "I am now experiencing this fruit of that previous karma.
This is because there would be no confidence even in the mere possibility that "some will be so," and because there is a lack of evidence for a definitive determination.

If it is argued that there is confidence regarding Kapila and others because they were like a group of teachers who, having slept through the night and awakened at dawn, mutually corroborate their teachings, this is not so; for just as there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for connecting one birth with another, there is likewise no such connection between different births. Furthermore, even if such a connection existed, since specific qualifications such as being a Brahmin would not be remembered across lives, there could be no confidence in the form of ritual performance.

For there is no rule that because the parents were Brāhmaṇas in a previous birth, their offspring must necessarily be Brāhmaṇas in a subsequent one; by which [rule] there could be an establishment of the distinctions of castes and so forth at the beginning of creation. [This would be impossible], as in the case of the Lord (Īśvara), who possesses specific elements bound by specific unseen forces (adṛṣṭa).
Because they are not perceived,
and because it has already been stated that there can be no confidence in the capacity to perceive supersensuous objects;
by this, the claim that the tradition is maintained through a system of colors associated with those who travel to other cosmic eggs is also refuted, due to the absence of any power for such travel.
For even traveling between different rain-clouds is difficult;
how much more so is traveling between different worlds, and how much more so is going to another cosmic egg?
If it is argued that "this might still be the case even for one who has attained powers such as *aṇimā*," we say no;
for there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) for this either,
and confidence cannot be established on the basis of mere possibility alone.
(152) If it is argued that the very impossibility of accounting for the universal acceptance [of the Veda] by the great masses of people is the proof here, we say no—
(153) because when the matter can be accounted for by the postulation of a single such [creator], the postulation of further [entities] would entail the fault of theoretical complexity (*gaurava*).
Furthermore, one must necessarily admit the power of creating bodies without a physical frame (*videha-nirmāṇa-śakti*) and the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth.
If it is argued that there must be only one [author], then there can be no confidence in anything other than God.
Furthermore: "Let the decline of the tradition be inferred from the observed decline in birth, sacramental rites, knowledge, capacity, Vedic study, and ritual action. (3)
For in the beginning, beings were born of pride;
thereafter, they came into existence through sexual union, with offspring as their sole purpose;
then [came] desire.

They arise from proximity to things that ought to be avoided; nowadays, due to the conditions of place, time, and so forth, they are for the most part derived solely from animal sacrifice (*paśudharma*).
Formerly, however, they were ritual refinements (*saṃskāra*) applied to sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and other such offerings. (121)
They will be established;
then, starting from the field;
then, starting from the womb.
But now,
since [the Vedas] have been lost, we rely on worldly convention;
previously, the Veda was studied in its thousand branches.
Then it was divided;
then there was one [school] with six branches;
but now, however, in some places there is only a single branch.
(122) Formerly, the Brahmins shone forth as those whose livelihood was truth; then, those whose livelihood was untruth;
(123) then, those whose livelihood was death.

At present, the livelihoods of those who live by falsehood, untruth, usury, cattle-rearing, and the service of horses have become predominant. Formerly, guests were received with difficulty by the Brahmins.
Then they became guests of the Kṣatriyas; then they even entered among the Vaiśyas; and now they have become eaters of the food of Śūdras as well.
After that, those who eat the remnants of offerings (vighasa-bhuj); after that, those who eat cooked food (anna-bhuj);
at present, there are only those who eat sin (aghā-bhuj).
Formerly, the Dharma had four quarters; then, as austerity declined, it became three-quartered;
then, as knowledge faded, it became two-quartered.

At present, the sacrifice is decaying; its sole remaining pillar, *dāna* (giving), stands unsteady due to hundreds of ailments such as "ill-gotten wealth" (*durāgata*). It is stained by the impurity of lack of faith (*aśraddhā*), shattered by hundreds of thorns such as desire and anger, and, with its strength diminishing day by day, it appears as if it were stumbling here and there.

If it is argued that "just as it is now, so it was always; no more than what is seen in the examples is required," we say no—because we observe the disappearance of those Vedic branches (śākhās) which were inferred from the practice of the Smṛtis;
because the authority of the Smṛtis and of custom is not admitted independently [of the Vedas];
and because there is no evidence for Manu and others having perceived supersensuous objects.

If one were to accept that the Smṛti arises from Ācāra and Ācāra arises from the Smṛti, there would follow the fallacy of a blind tradition (*andhaparamparā*) due to the assumption of beginninglessness; furthermore,
since that which has not been recited since the beginning of saṃsāra cannot be established as the Veda, inference is impossible.
Because a mere sequence of phonemes that is not delimited by [context] is meaningless, whether in terms of its origin, its manifestation, or its intended meaning.
And if it is inferred that "this is a means to achieve welfare" or "this ought to be done" because it is the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), [then...]
What is the use of inferring the Veda?
For its meaning is established through inference itself.
Nor is this very inference the object of inference because it is the cognition of dharma; rather, the Veda is the object of inference.
Because it is established by direct perception and because it is not based on scripture.

If it is argued that this [practice] is rooted in a means of valid cognition because it is the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), then that results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Because it is accepted that [the Veda] has perception as its basis, and because even in the absence of that [perception], inference is possible.
If it is argued: "Since it is eternally unknown, how can it be non-informative, and how can it be an inference or a basis?"—[we reply: Is the Veda informative while remaining unknown?
Or rather, the root [of inference] is simply that which does not itself produce cognition,
which is why you hold it to be the most insentient thing.
If you argue that it must be something known because it is itself inferred, then let the inferential mark (liṅga) be exactly like that as well.
If it is argued that the cognition of the logical mark (*liṅga*) prior to the cognition of the object to be inferred is required because it is the cause,
whereas a subsequent cognition is not— then the same applies to the cognition of the word (*śabda*).

[Objection: It is inferred that the nature of conduct has its root in verbal testimony (śabda), and by that verbal testimony, the status of being something to be done (kartavyatā) is understood. [Reply: This is not so—because the nature of conduct is established through direct perception (pratyakṣa) and thus does not depend on any other source.
Therefore, since there is no perception of it as something to be done, [it cannot be established by verbal testimony].
And because there is no scope for verbal testimony or inference due to the lack of measurement [of the agent],

and because direct perception and revealed scripture are impossible, one infers the duty to act solely by way of the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*), and through that, one infers the underlying verbal testimony.
And so, what is the use of it? For its object has already been established.
Nevertheless, its very basis remains the scripture (*āgama*).
If it is argued that this is because of pervasion (*vyāpti*), then for that very reason, one must infer that its basis is perception and inference.
If it is argued that while [the world] would have a beginning, this [practice] is beginningless—[we reply: so too is conduct (*ācāra*). (130)
In that case, this [particular instance] would be the very first,
whereas this [practice] would be beginningless even without scripture.
Let there be such beginninglessness for both the performance of the practice and the inference [of it].
If you ask, "What is lost for us?"—first, the claim that "the Veda is eternally inferable," and second, the claim that "teaching alone is the authority regarding Dharma.
(131) Now, this is the underlying intention: even Vedic practices, such as the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices, are seen to be undergoing total extinction.
For these [rites] are not performed now,

yet it is not the case that they were never performed even previously; otherwise, it would follow that the entire body of the Veda, whose purpose consists of those rites, lacks authority, like an instruction on crossing the ocean [when no one actually crosses].
And let it not be so,
because [the case here] shares the same logical status as the instruction regarding the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*) and other rites.
Thus, furthermore, there will be some time [in the future].
Where these will be practiced,
so too other customs (ācāras) will likewise be abolished and practiced.
Thus, there is no interruption [of the tradition].

If it is argued that, for that reason, [the practice] is rooted in scripture (*āgama*), then, in that case, since there would be no inference of either the duty (*kartavyatva*) or the scripture in the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*) at the beginning of the lineage, and since there is no direct revelation (*pratyakṣaśruti*), how could even the discussion of conduct (*ācārasaṅkathā*) exist? Consequently, everything would collapse.
Therefore, direct Vedic revelation alone is the root of traditional practice (*ācāra*);
if that no longer exists now, it follows that the Vedic branches (*śākhā*) have been lost.
If it is argued that it still exists elsewhere even now—then why does it not exist here?
Is it because the lineages of the teachers have departed elsewhere, or because they themselves have been extinguished, or rather because of the interruption of the study of the Vedas?
It cannot be the first or the second [alternative],
because if all [persons] were to go elsewhere or perish, it would necessarily follow that the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) in Bhāratavarṣa would also perish,
since that [conduct] has as its agent the same person who is the student [of the Veda].
If the practice of study were to occur through the introduction of conduct by those who have come from elsewhere, that might be possible;
however, the third alternative is not tenable, because it is impossible as long as there is no interruption of disciples endowed with internal spiritual power.

Therefore, because the capacity for longevity, health, strength, vigor, faith, tranquility, self-restraint, comprehension, retention, and so forth, diminishes day by day, and because the practice of one's own Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) is wasting away, we consider it logical that these two [the Vedas and their practices] somehow continue; furthermore, due to the universal adoption [of traditions], the total eradication of everything does not occur all at once.
(134) Since "the world follows what has gone before," such a practice is indeed devoid of any authoritative basis.

If it is argued that there is no destruction of the Vedic branches (*śākhoccheda*), because since the procedural details (*itikartavyatā*) must be supplied from many branches, there would otherwise follow a lack of confidence even regarding a single ritual action— [we reply: No, for in this way,
the very acceptance (*parigraha*) by the great multitude of people would be subject to subversion.
If the Vedas too were accepted by people merely out of blind conformity (*gatānugatikatā*),
they would not be authoritative;
thus, it would be like one fleeing from the fear of a scorpion falling into the mouth of a venomous snake.

And it was precisely for this reason— that they apprehended the lack of security resulting from the eventual destruction of the Śākya lineage that would occur in the course of time— that the great seers provided a remedy.
Therefore, even the aforementioned fault does not apply;
nor is this annihilation achieved through a sequence of cognitions,
by which it might be praiseworthy.
Rather, it proceeds through the sequence of the ripening of negligence, intoxication, pride, indolence,
and nihilism; then, following that, there is again a flow, and immediately after that, once more annihilation— like the current of the Sarasvatī river.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the loss of what has been done (*kṛtahāna*).

And thus, even though this [world] exists like a future stream, it is inferred to be preceded by annihilation. Furthermore, the Blessed One Vyāsa records the word of the Lord in the *Gītā*: "Whenever, O Bhārata, there is a decline of Dharma..."
When there is the rise of unrighteousness, then I manifest myself.
For the protection of the virtuous, for the destruction of the evil-doers,
and for the sake of establishing righteousness, I manifest myself age after age.
Thus it is said in the *Bhagavadgītā* (4.7–8).
But what is this "acceptance by the great multitude" (*mahājanaparigraha*)?
It is the acceptance, retention, exposition, and practice [of a teaching] by those who are devoid of the perception of a [valid] logical reason (*hetudarśanaśūnya*).
For he would not exist here without a cause;
for in this case, laziness and the like are not the cause, because [the world] is primarily characterized by karma consisting of suffering.
Nor is there entry into this [system] out of necessity due to a lack of qualification for other means whose validity is established,
for even those honored by others do not enter here;
nor is it out of passion for the non-duality of food, drink, and so forth.
This is because it is devoted to establishing the systematic classification of those [categories];
nor is there any delusion caused by the impact of practicing fallacious reasoning, since this has been practiced from childhood.
Nor is there association with heretics who are prone to deception,
because [the practice] proceeds through the lineage of one's father and so forth;
nor is there an intention for non-distraction based on the conceit of practicing yoga.
Because the beginner is exceedingly preoccupied with the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa),
nor is it for the sake of a livelihood.
Because there is an absence of visible results according to the reasoning previously stated,
nor is it a case of deception by trickery,
since that is impossible in the present context.
[2.280] However, these reasons are possible for the acceptance of the scriptures of the Buddhists and others. For instance:

the fact that there is a great lightness of ritual action therein appeals to the indolent; the fact that even those fallen from this [path] may enter appeals to those who have no other resort; the fact that there are no restrictions regarding food and so forth appeals to the passionate; and [the fact of] acting according to one's own will...

"Seizers" refers to those who practice fallacious reasoning; "those associated with heretics" refers to those who claim that activity proceeds from the absence of a lineage of fathers and so forth; "those who pride themselves on being undistracted" refers to those who cite such scriptural passages as, "Having understood the difference between the two, for whom is purity prescribed?"; "the unfit" refers to those for whom [the teaching] is a livelihood, based on the accomplishment of eating at seven *ghaṭikās* and so forth; and "the paralyzing of the sun" and "the splitting of stones."
The breaking of branches,
possession by spirits,
and the speaking of images.

Regarding the phrase "alchemical theory" (*dhātuvāda*) and so forth: because of their delusion (*dhandhana*, i.e., deception), it is conceivable that they embrace those who have been cheated by such frauds. (144)
Therefore, the distinction is that they are not embraced by the great multitude.
It might be argued: "If this were so, there would be a contradiction in the functioning of all karma, and nothing at all would arise."

Since nothing whatsoever perishes, in a world resembling still, motionless space, from what specific cause could there be a new creation? The Sāṅkhyas' claim that it arises from the transformation of *prakṛti* is plausible;
the followers of Bhāskara's school find it appropriate to say it arises from the transformation of Brahman.
The claim that it arises "from the ripening of latent impressions" (vāsanāparipākāt) follows the Buddhist doctrine.
Furthermore, the claim that it arises "from a specific time" (kālaviśeṣāt) is untenable because there is no specific limiting condition (upādhi);
moreover, non-existent secondary characteristics cannot function as qualifiers.
Because it is always of an identical nature;
nor is it by way of cognition,
since that [cognition], being impermanent, is absent at that time.

If it is argued that this is because there is no distinction for the eternal [atoms], whether in terms of their objects or their essential nature—we say no. Just as the continuous flow of breaths—which has as its sole purpose the accomplishment of the sequence of the maturation of the lifespan of living beings who have fallen asleep due to the fatigue of bodily agitation—continues; so too, for atoms which have acquired latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) through the agitation of the dissolution of the great elements, there exists a process culminating in the conjunction known as "accumulation" (*pracaya*), whose sole purpose is the delimitation of time by degrees of slowness, greater slowness, and so forth.
Because the continuum of karma proceeds as the breath of the Lord,
as for the question "how long does it last?", since there is no contradiction, it is accepted that it lasts for exactly that duration, without overstepping what is well-known from scripture.
Alternatively, the activity within other cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) serves as the limiting adjunct for time;
when time is delimited by that [activity], creation occurs again.
This is just as fruits are spread out upon a gourd vine.
Likewise, it is heard in scripture that thousands of cosmic eggs (*aṇḍa*) are pervaded by the power of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).
(145) Such being the case, when separation is possible, whose [Veda] is accepted by whom, such that its authority might be established?
This matter is indicative (*jñāpaka*), not productive (*kāraka*).
Therefore, since the effect would cease for want of a producer, how could that which is intended to be indicative establish it?
There are indeed Kapila and others who have directly realized *dharma* and are perfected through the yoga of action.
Seeing living beings thus being cooked in the coals of saṃsāra, those who are supremely compassionate will favor them by teaching what is pleasing and beneficial.

If it is argued that this has already been accomplished by the Supreme Lord—who, like one indifferent to knowing the number of insects and such—[we reply]: No, because there is no confidence in anyone other than Him.

For instance, even if one accepts that meditation (*bhāvanā*) is the means for perceiving supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārtha*), it does not produce a truly real direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*), because of which we feel confident. If it is argued that this is due to corroboration by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [we reply]— no— [as is the case with] non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth.

(147) Because that [means of achieving welfare] is absent in the case of [the claim] "it is a means for achieving welfare. If it is argued that there is scripture (*āgama*) [to support this], we say no; for since its very root is mere mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it too is an object of lack of confidence.
If it is argued that activity [proceeds] even through partial correspondence, we say no—(148)
Because it is possible for things to occur otherwise, as in the case of recounting a dream;
furthermore, there can be no cultivation of what has not been perceived,
for only thieves, snakes, and the like that have been perceived are cultivated by those who are fearful.
Furthermore, the fact that ritual action (karman) and yoga are means for achieving one's welfare has not been established from any source;
nor is the perception of their essential nature (svarūpa) of any practical utility anywhere.
Or [it may be] that which is to be accomplished through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
However, neither positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is possible in this case,
because the fruit is to be realized in another body.
Because it is not well-known, it is not practiced;
and because of that lack of practice, it does not exist.
Nor can that [rebirth] be established merely through the linking of two bodies— one as an agent and the other as an enjoyer—
because such a link is absent.
For no one links [the two experiences] by thinking, "I am now experiencing this fruit of that previous karma."
Because there is no confidence even in the mere possibility that "some will be so," as there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such a definitive determination; and because,

like a teacher who falls asleep at night and wakes up in the morning to find all his students repeating what he taught, there is no basis for confidence in Kapila and others based on mutual corroboration— just as there is no confidence in the continuity of a single birth, there is likewise none in the continuity of another birth.
Because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge [to establish it].

Furthermore, even so, since there is no recollection of one's status as a Brahmin and so forth due to the specific nature of the qualified agent, there would be a lack of confidence regarding the performance [of rituals].
Indeed, there is no rule that because the parents were Brahmins in a previous birth, one is a Brahmin in the subsequent one.
By which [cause] there could be an establishment of the distinctions of castes and other attributes at the beginning of creation;
for, unlike the case of Īśvara, no distinction among the specific elements (or their differences) bound by a particular *adṛṣṭa* is perceived.

Furthermore, since it has already been stated that there is no basis for confidence in the capacity to perceive objects beyond the senses, this refutes the claim that the tradition was established through the systematic movement of colors between different cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*); for such power of movement does not exist.
Indeed, even traveling to another continent is difficult enough.
Whence could there be movement to another world? And how much less, the journey to another cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)?
If it is argued that this might still be possible through the attainment of powers such as *aṇimā* (minuteness), we say no—(151)
Because here too there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*),
and because confidence cannot be established on the basis of mere probability (*sambhāvanā*) alone.
(152) If it is argued that the very fact that [the doctrine] is accepted by the great multitude (*mahājana*) is itself the valid evidence here, we say no— (153)

Since the [required] establishment is possible through such a single conceptualization alone, there would be the consequence of unnecessary complexity (gaurava) in postulating further conceptualizations;
moreover, the power of creating bodies without a physical frame and the sovereign powers such as *aṇimā* must necessarily be admitted.
If it is argued that "let there be only one [such power]," we reply: in that case, there can be no confidence in anything other than God (*īśvara*).

Repeatedly creating this world, which consists of extraordinary wonders through the power of illusion, and repeatedly withdrawing it as if it were a magician’s trick, He plays with the universe like a game of Indra-jāla.
Bowing before that god Śiva— the source of all trust, the embodiment of existence, and the power of whose unrestrained, radiant meditation is manifest—
may I remain so even in my final moments. (4)
Thus ends the second chapter in the Nyāyakusumāñjali.
